extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of biology, history, and the philosophy/methods of science (historians, anthropologists, sociologists, biologists, and educated general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on interpreting human history and social institutions using principles of natural selection and scientific method; includes methodological criteria for making historical inquiry scientific and for classifying sciences. Emphasizes which factors must be attended to when applying evolution to social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: History must yield sequences resumable in scientific formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: "History can never become science, can never be aught but a catalogue of facts rehearsed... until these facts are seen to fall into sequences which can be briefly resumed in scientific formulae."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make historical study scientific, facts should be organized into lawful sequences expressible in concise conceptual shorthand; only then does history move from narrative to science and gain predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate change by tracing one social unit through time
rubrics_metrics.description: "To find sequences of facts — a growth or evolution expressible by a scientific law — we must follow the changes of one tribe or people at a time. We cannot trace the successive stages of social life except by the minute investigation of facts relating to one social unit, which may... be afterwards compared with like investigations for other units."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological prescription for historical-scientific work: conduct detailed, unit-level longitudinal studies, then compare across units to infer general laws. Labeled as the remedy for 'good theory and bad practice' in historical investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive history describable by evolutionary principles using comparative data
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is peculiarly in 'prehistoric history' that we are for the time being best able to apply the scientific method... The earliest history of each individual people follows general laws of human development which are capable of accurate scientific statement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative anthropology, folklore, and mythology; focus on average results over long periods and large areas to detect common developmental sequences despite local variation due to environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and sexual factors as fundamental explanatory variables for social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The growth of national and social life... The economical condition of any nation... is closely associated with its rate of reproductivity and with its indirect struggle against its neighbours for land and food... the continual variations in these forms are in modern history usually hidden under problems of trade and exchange... It is this struggle which is the fundamental formula for the description of all existing systems of ownership and of marriage in its widest sense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of ownership, marriage, family structure, and related institutions should foreground food/economic pressures and sexual instincts as primary drivers; treat other legal/statistical manifestations as disguises of these underlying factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific history should aim to predict future social tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: "When we have learned to describe the sequences of primitive history in terms of physical and biological formulae, then we shall hesitate less to dig deep down into our modern civilization and find its roots... We shall then be less unwilling to admit that historical science... is capable of predicting the future course of development."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political economy and sociology are legitimate predictive sciences when founded on historically-derived economic and social regularities; historical science's aim includes forecasting probable tendencies from past data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biologists must define the limits of applicability of natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "Biologists are called upon to define the limits within which they suppose the formula of natural selection to be a valid description: in particular, how it is related to that physical selection of more stable inorganic compounds... At the other end of the scale we have again to ask how far the survival of the fittest describes the sequences of human history."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Darwinian concepts, explicitly state the domain and boundaries of applicability (e.g., relation to physical selection, to prebiotic chemistry, and to social/historical processes) rather than assuming universal applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for multiple levels/factors of selection: Individualism, Socialism, and Humanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "The struggle for existence involves not only the struggle of individual man against individual man, but also the struggle of individual society against individual society, as well as the struggle of the totality of humanity with its organic and inorganic environment... If our analysis has been a correct one it has led us... to three great factors — Individualism, Socialism, and Humanism — tending to modify human life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of human evolution or social change must include multi-level selection and interacting tendencies: individual self-advancement, social/tribal organization and collective training (socialism in the author's sense), and broader human solidarity (humanism). Neglecting group- or species-level factors yields an incomplete account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social organization and training of social instincts are necessary for societal survival and moral sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The interest individual societies have in educating, training, and organizing the powers of all their individual members... this tendency to social organization... may be termed Socialism... It is the prevalence of social instinct in the dominant portion of a given community which is the sole and yet perfectly efficient sanction to the observance of social, that is moral, lines of conduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative-methodological claim: to explain or promote stable societies, emphasize mechanisms of social training, state-led organization, and development of tribal/social conscience; these are both explananda in evolutionary history and prescriptions for social policy in the author's analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish life from non-life by structural and motion characteristics, not consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The distinction between living and lifeless is not capable of brief definition, consciousness and self-determination give us no assistance, and we are thrown back on special characteristics of structure and motion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining or studying life scientifically, focus on measurable structural and dynamic properties rather than vague metaphysical notions like consciousness; accept that brief definitions may fail and emphasize operational characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science is primarily description (conceptual shorthand) aimed at prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Knowledge is essentially a description and not an explanation — that the object of science is to describe in conceptual shorthand the routine of our past experience, with a view of predicting the future."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific work should construct concise conceptual indices (formulae, laws) that summarize past phenomena and provide predictive leverage; explanation in metaphysical terms is cautioned against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sciences should be grounded in psychological/associative processes (conceptions index impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The work of science viewed from the psychological standpoint is thus essentially that of association... From the stored sense-impresses we form by association conceptions... These conceptions are... ideal symbols, conceptual shorthand by aid of which we index or classify immediate sense-impressions, stored sense-impresses, or other conceptions themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or organizing scientific disciplines, attend to how concepts function as indexing tools for sensory and stored impressions; scientific classification is an activity of creating conceptual shorthand that maps onto cognitive associative structure.
